title: Accuracy of Noise Ceiling Estimators for Brain Scores
claim: Recorded responses are modeled as shared signals plus trial-specific signals, mixed by misaligned weights, with added Gaussian noise.
layout: 4 panels, signals on left, equation top right, spatial grids bottom right
description: The figure shows how simulated brain-recording trials are generated. Panel (a), top left, builds a smooth signal by convolving Poisson events of exponential duration (a rectangular pulse train) with a hemodynamic response function curve. This gives a smooth wiggly trace labelled phi_k. Panel (b), bottom left, shows a jagged random trace phi_k, which stands for an i.i.d. Gaussian process. Panel (c), top right, is an equation: v^(l) equals a T×K matrix of shared and trial-specific signal columns (pink, blue, green, with ellipses), times mixing weights W^(l) (K×X×Y), plus Gaussian noise N(0, sigma²). Panel (d), bottom right, shows two X×Y grids as heatmaps. Blue, green and red blobs on the first grid appear shifted or recolored on the second. An arrow between them is labelled 'Different trial-specific signals, shifted mixing weights'.
caption: Signal and trial generation. (a) To mimic the fMRI BOLD response to a continuous stimulus, signals are generated by convolving an event time series with the hemodynamic response function (HRF). (b) To mimic the response to a set of randomly ordered discrete stimuli, signals are generated as i.i.d. Gaussian processes. (c) A trial is generated by multiplying shared and trial-specific signals with trial-specific mixing weights, and adding Gaussian noise. (d) Two generated trials differ by their trial-specific signals and their (potentially) misaligned mixing weights. More details about the generative process are provided in Sec. [ref].
abstract: The internal activations of modern machine learning models align surprisingly well with the activities recorded in real brains. In the last five years, the alignment between encoding models and brain activities, often called brain scores, has steadily increased. Because brain recordings are noisy, there exists an upper bound to the brain scores that any model can achieve. This bound, called the noise ceiling, is crucial for two reasons: it determines whether further improvements in model performance are possible, and it enables meaningful comparisons of brain scores across benchmarks. The field has developed multiple approaches to estimate noise ceilings, but the statistical properties of existing estimators remain poorly understood, leaving it unclear in which experimental settings they provide reliable estimates. Here, we introduce a unified mathematical framework for brain recordings, use it to derive closed-form expressions for four commonly used noise ceiling estimators, and provide theoretical predictions for the behavior of each estimator. We validate the theoretical predictions with simulations that we compare to noise ceiling estimates in existing fMRI and EEG datasets. We find that the existing methods underestimate the true noise ceiling in different settings. We conclude with recommendations for best practice in different situations.
